name: libaco
baseline: none named (no baseline in README; ucontext implied by 'fastest' claim)
workload: Context switch between asymmetric coroutines (acosw), standalone stack, 20M resume/yield loop, x86-64.
claimed_speedup: About 10.29 ns per context switch (10.38 ns with per-coroutine FPU/MXCSR words); 10M coroutines in 2.8 GB with copy-stack at 120 B each.
tradeoffs: Asymmetric only; x86-64 and i386 only (no arm64); must call aco_exit instead of return; one instance per thread; optional shared-stack copying.
caveats: First-party numbers, no comparison against libco or Boost.Context in the README; 'fastest' defined only as fastest Sys V ABI compliant switch. Compiler flags not stated in the page part read. Dated 2018.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Libaco: A fast and lightweight C asymmetric coroutine library' (item 17528735), also surfaced by query 'Show HN stackful coroutines C context switch faster than boost.context libco'

name: Neco
baseline: none named (README claims fast switching; ucontext fallback only)
workload: Stackful symmetric coroutines with built-in scheduler and I/O; context switch time.
claimed_speedup: About 11 ns per context switch (via llco assembly).
tradeoffs: Single scheduler per thread; pthread mutex/cond do not work well inside coroutines; Windows and WebAssembly support incomplete; Linux/macOS/BSD focus.
caveats: First-party, single number, no baseline library compared, no flags stated. Context switch is inherited from llco/minicoro assembly.

name: llco
workload: Low-level stackful coroutine switch (assembly adapted from minicoro and Lua Coco); powers neco and sco.
claimed_speedup: Claims fast assembly context switching with ucontext fallback; no numbers in README as read.
license: Unlicense OR MIT-0 (README: Public Domain or MIT No Attribution)
tradeoffs: No scheduler; caller supplies stack; Windows x86_64 only; WebAssembly needs -sASYNCIFY.
caveats: No benchmark numbers found; evidence is directional only. Listed because neco's 11 ns figure comes from it.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN: Neco' (item 39971984) led to llco

name: minicoro
baseline: ucontext (in own table; not in list)
workload: CPU cycles per context switch, init and uninit for the assembly, ucontext and Windows fiber backends.
claimed_speedup: x86_64 Linux: assembly 9 cycles per switch vs ucontext 352 cycles (about 39x, derived from page data); Windows assembly 33 cycles vs fibers 69.
hardware: Intel Core i7-8750H @ 2.20 GHz, preallocated coroutines
license: Unlicense OR MIT-0 (README: Public Domain or MIT No Attribution)
tradeoffs: Asymmetric Lua-style coroutines; single header; fixed stack size per coroutine; header is C but usable from C++.
caveats: Author's own benchmark table; compiler and flags not stated; no Boost.Context or libco row. 9 cycles probably excludes scheduler work.
found_via: Hacker News: surfaced via 'Show HN lightweight stackful coroutines C++ header-only' search (thread: 'You can roll stackful coroutines in C++ (or C) with 50-ish lines of Assembly', item 47515896, mentions minicoro)

name: coros-fibers
workload: Coroutine/fiber context switch rate on x86-64, low-level coro_transfer and fiber scheduler.
claimed_speedup: 58 to 62 million context switches/s with coro_transfer/coro_restore (about 16-17 ns); 21 million switches/s through fibers scheduler.
tradeoffs: x86-64 only; low-level coro API plus scheduler; author says tracking fewer registers could be faster but breaks ABI.
caveats: Old, first-party, no comparison, no compiler flags. Based on the libcoro transfer design.
found_via: Hacker News: comment 'This is a C++ coroutines framework (github.com/markpapadakis/coros-fibers)' (item 13201024)

name: Coros
baseline: Intel oneTBB / libfork (README compares via graphs; not in baseline list)
workload: Fork-join task parallelism with C++20 coroutines and continuation stealing: Fibonacci(30) scheduling overhead and matrix multiplication.
claimed_speedup: README shows graphs only (images/graph_w1.png etc.); no numeric speedup text.
tradeoffs: Needs C++23 (std::expected); stackless coroutines, so not a Boost.Context replacement; own ThreadPool.
caveats: Benchmark results are images only and could not be read; no baseline numbers or flags. Task-parallelism library, only loosely this category (libfork is already catalogued).
